options.explanation: Right. SwiftUI views are lightweight structs that conform to View.

options.explanation: SwiftUI views are value-type structs, not UIKit UIView classes.

options.text: An enum case that holds layout numbers and colors.
options.explanation: Views are structs with a body property, not enum cases.

options.text: An actor that moves UI drawing onto background worker threads.
options.explanation: Views are not actors. SwiftUI updates the UI on the main thread.

questions.prompt: Why are SwiftUI views built as structs instead of classes?

options.text: Because Swift classes cannot conform to custom protocols.
options.explanation: Classes can conform to protocols normally in Swift.

options.text: Because structs are lightweight value types that SwiftUI recreates fast.
options.explanation: Right. Structs avoid reference counting overhead, so SwiftUI can recreate them fast.

options.text: Because structs let multiple screens share the same object in memory.
options.explanation: Structs copy values on assignment instead of sharing one reference.

options.text: Because classes cannot draw icons, images, or text on screen.
options.explanation: Classes can draw UI. Structs are chosen because value types are fast to recreate.

questions.prompt: What does a view modifier do when you call it on a SwiftUI view?

options.text: It changes the existing view struct in place on the screen.
options.explanation: Views are immutable structs and cannot be changed in place.

options.text: It removes the old view and pushes a new screen automatically.
options.explanation: Modifiers style or lay out views. They do not change navigation.

options.text: It wraps the existing view inside a new view struct layer.
options.explanation: Right. Each modifier returns a new wrapper view such as ModifiedContent.

options.text: It starts a background timer that checks for color changes.
options.explanation: Modifiers wrap views for layout and style. They do not start timers.

questions.prompt: Why does the order of view modifiers matter in SwiftUI?

options.text: Because the Swift compiler sorts modifiers in alphabetical order.
options.explanation: Swift runs modifier chains in the exact order you write them.

options.text: Because modifiers run at the same time on separate background queues.
options.explanation: Modifiers build a layered view tree in order, not on background queues.

options.text: Because background modifiers always erase earlier size modifiers.
options.explanation: Background modifiers wrap earlier sizes without erasing them.

options.text: Because each modifier wraps the previous view in a new layer.
options.explanation: Right. Each modifier wraps the layer before it, so order changes the layout.

questions.prompt: What generic wrapper type does SwiftUI create when you chain modifiers?

options.text: AnyView, which hides all view types at compile time.
options.explanation: SwiftUI keeps exact types and only uses AnyView when you ask for it.

options.text: UIViewWrapper, which links SwiftUI views to UIKit layers.
options.explanation: SwiftUI wraps views in ModifiedContent, not UIViewWrapper.

options.text: ViewModifier, which holds mutable app data between launches.
options.explanation: ViewModifier is a protocol for styling views, not a storage wrapper.

options.text: ModifiedContent, which wraps the content view and modifier type.
options.explanation: Right. ModifiedContent<Content, Modifier> is the generic wrapper type.

questions.prompt: Explain why SwiftUI views are declared as structs instead of reference classes. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that SwiftUI views are lightweight descriptions of the screen, not permanent UI objects.
States that structs are value types with no reference counting overhead.
Explains that cheap recreation lets SwiftUI rebuild and diff view trees often.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI views are lightweight descriptions of the screen, not permanent objects like UIKit views. Because views are structs, they are value types with no reference counting overhead. SwiftUI can create and discard thousands of them fast whenever state changes. It then diffs the new view tree against the old one to update only what changed.

questions.prompt: Explain why modifier order matters in SwiftUI, and give an example showing how reversing the order changes the layout. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that modifiers do not change a view in place, but wrap it in a new layer.
Gives an example comparing .padding().background() with .background().padding().
Describes the visual result: coloring the padded box versus coloring only the tight text.

questions.modelAnswer: In SwiftUI, modifiers do not change a view in place. Each modifier wraps the layer before it inside a new view container. Because of this wrapping, order changes what appears on screen. For example, .padding().background(.blue) adds space first and paints the whole padded box blue. Reversing it to .background(.blue).padding() paints only the tight text blue and leaves clear space outside.

questions.prompt: What does the return type some View mean on the body property, and why is it used? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Identifies some View as an opaque return type.
Explains that it hides long nested generic modifier types such as ModifiedContent.
States that it keeps compile-time type safety so SwiftUI can diff the view tree.

questions.modelAnswer: The return type some View is an opaque return type. When you chain modifiers, SwiftUI builds deep generic types like ModifiedContent. Writing those long types by hand would make code hard to read and easy to break. Using some View hides the nested wrapper type from your code while letting the compiler keep the exact concrete type for safe diffing.

questions.prompt: How do you build a custom ViewModifier in SwiftUI, and how do you make it easy to call? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Creates a struct conforming to the ViewModifier protocol.
Implements func body(content: Content) -> some View to style content.
Adds an extension on View so callers can use clean dot syntax.

questions.modelAnswer: To build a custom modifier, declare a struct that conforms to the ViewModifier protocol. Implement func body(content: Content) -> some View and chain your styling modifiers onto content. To make it easy to call, write an extension on View with a helper method that returns modifier(MyModifier()). Other views can then apply the style using normal dot syntax.

questions.prompt: Why should you never run slow tasks or network calls inside var body? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that SwiftUI evaluates var body often on the main thread when inputs or state change.
States that slow work inside body blocks the main thread and causes dropped frames.
Explains that body should stay fast and only describe what the screen should show.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI reads var body often on the main thread whenever inputs or state change. If you put network calls, large database reads, or slow loops inside body, they run during UI updates. Slow work blocks the main thread, which causes dropped frames and a frozen screen. Keep var body fast and pure so it only describes the view layout.
